topic: DP-3T: The Invisible Shield of Privacy in Contact Tracing
target_audience: University students (Computer Science, Cybersecurity, or Public Health Tech)

sections.title: The Privacy Paradox: Contact Tracing vs. Surveillance
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of digital contact tracing during a pandemic. Explain the tension between needing to track virus spread and protecting individual location privacy. Introduce the goal of DP-3T: finding out if you were near an infected person without a central authority knowing your identity or location.
sections.example: Imagine Alice and Bob meet in a park. We want Bob to get an alert if Alice tests positive, but we don't want a government server to know Alice and Bob were at the park at 2:00 PM.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Bluetooth BLE and Hashing
sections.content: Briefly explain two foundational concepts: 1. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) 'Beacons' (short-range signals). 2. Cryptographic Hash Functions (one-way functions that turn data into unique digital fingerprints).
sections.example: Visual: A smartphone emitting a faint blue circle (BLE range). A 'meat grinder' animation showing a Secret Key being turned into a random-looking string of numbers (Hashing).

sections.title: Step 1: Generating Ephemeral IDs (The Rotating Mask)
sections.content: Every day, Alice's phone generates a new Secret Key ($SK_t$). From this key, it generates 'EpsID' (Ephemeral IDs) that change every 15 minutes using a hash function. This ensures that even if someone intercepts a signal, they can't track Alice across different times of the day.
sections.example: Alice's phone calculates $EpsID = Hash(SK_t || 	ext{Time Slot})$. Visual: Alice's phone 'whispers' a code like 'A1B2', then 15 minutes later, it 'whispers' 'C3D4'.

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Local Storage)
sections.content: When Alice and Bob are near each other, their phones exchange their current $EpsIDs$ via Bluetooth. Crucially, these IDs are stored ONLY on their respective devices in a local log. The server knows nothing about this interaction.
sections.example: Visual: Bob's phone sees Alice's 'A1B2' and puts it into a private digital 'shoebox' labeled 'Seen Today'. Alice does the same with Bob's ID.

sections.title: Step 3: The Diagnosis Report (Sharing the Key, Not the Contacts)
sections.content: If Alice tests positive, she uploads her Secret Key ($SK_t$) for that day to a central server. She does NOT upload the list of people she met. The server then publishes a list of keys from infected people to all users.
sections.example: Visual: Alice sends a single 'Golden Key' to a public bulletin board. The bulletin board now lists 'Key-Alice-Day5'. It doesn't mention Bob or any location.

sections.title: Step 4: Local Matching (The Privacy Win)
sections.content: Every user's phone periodically downloads the new 'infected keys' from the server. Bob's phone takes Alice's $SK_t$ and re-calculates all possible $EpsIDs$ Alice would have broadcasted that day. It then compares these to the IDs stored in Bob's local 'shoebox'.
sections.example: Visual: Bob's phone runs a quick calculation: 'Does $Hash(Key	ext{-Alice-Day5})$ match any ID in my shoebox? Yes! It matches A1B2!' Bob gets an alert: 'You may have been exposed.' The server still has no idea Bob exists.
